title: Risk assessment and hazard signage
audience: Cleaners working in or near laboratories where hazard signs and risk assessments apply.
learningOutcomes: Treat new hazard signage as a changed-condition trigger, not as something to interpret into permission.
Record the sign's location without approaching the hazard.
Route away and ask laboratory staff to revise the cleaning boundary.

instruction.heading: What a risk assessment is for a cleaner
instruction.body: A risk assessment is the record of what could hurt someone in a particular task, who could be hurt, and which controls reduce that risk. For a cleaner, the relevant assessment is the one written for the cleaning task in that laboratory, together with the site's hazard information. You do not write the laboratory's risk assessment, and you do not extend it on your own. Your job is to know the boundary it sets, to notice when the conditions have moved outside it, and to stop when they have. The service specification you were given is a snapshot taken on the day it was written. A laboratory changes its occupancy, its signage, its equipment and its procedures, and each change can alter what is safe to clean. Treat the assessment as a current document that must match the room you are standing in, not as a permission slip that stays valid until someone tells you otherwise.

instruction.heading: New signs are a changed condition
instruction.body: A new warning sign in a laboratory corridor is a change in the condition of the workplace. A service specification written before the sign was posted does not account for it. Treat the sign as a trigger to stop and reconfirm the boundary. The sign may mark a biological hazard, a chemical store, a radiation or laser area, a room that is being decommissioned, or a space that is awaiting an inspection. You will not know which from the sign alone, and you should not try to work it out by reading the sign closely. Do not decide for yourself what the sign means, and do not read it as permission to go in. The absence of a sign is not permission either, so a corridor that was open last week is only open this week if the site confirms it. The stop is not a judgement about the sign. It is a recognition that the job as written no longer describes the room.

instruction.heading: Keeping a distance while you record
instruction.body: Record the location of the sign from a safe distance, and note the time. Stand where you can see the sign and the entry point without moving closer to read small print or to look through a door panel. Note the corridor, the room number or the nearest landmark, the position of the sign on the door or wall, and what the sign shows in general terms, such as a symbol, a colour and any wording you can read from where you stand. Do not open doors, lift lids, look under benches or photograph inside a room. If a photograph is needed to make the location clear, take it only of the outside of the door and only if the site allows photographs in that area. Check the laboratory hazard map with the site management if it is available, and note any difference between the map and what you can see. Record what you observed, not what you assume the sign means.

instruction.heading: Routing away and asking for a revised boundary
instruction.body: Route away from the area by the way you came in, and keep other people away from it where you safely can. Do not stand in the corridor to wait for an answer if it puts you in the path of a hazard. Once you are clear, contact the laboratory staff or the site management and ask them to revise the cleaning boundary in writing. The written request should say what you saw, where, when, which part of the job is affected and what you need: an updated scope, a decision about the affected area, and any instructions for the rest of the job. A verbal answer in the corridor is not enough. The revised boundary must name the areas that are open, the areas that are closed, the people who decided and the time the decision was made. Until that written boundary arrives, the affected area stays out of the job and the rest of the job waits for the same confirmation.

instruction.heading: Returning to work after a stop
instruction.body: Resume only when the site authority has supplied an updated scope and you have been trained and equipped for the work it describes. If the new scope allows some areas but not others, clean only the areas named as open, and leave the rest untouched. The handover at the end of the job covers housekeeping only. It does not imply sterilisation, decontamination or clearance of any kind. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission states that claims about a business's services must be accurate and based on reasonable grounds, that a business must be able to prove the claims it makes, and that the rule covers statements made by staff as well as advertising. A handover that says a corridor is sterile, or that a sign no longer applies, would be a claim you cannot prove as a cleaner. Record what was tidied and what was not touched, and leave any other conclusion to the people who can test and decide it. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

instruction.heading: Worked boundary: one corridor, three signs
instruction.body: Consider a laboratory corridor with three doors. The service specification covers the general floor and two rooms that are open for housekeeping. A new sign now appears on the third door, and the floor plate outside the first room has a new yellow marking that does not appear on the plan. Under this lesson, the general floor and the two open rooms are still in scope only if the site confirms they are unchanged, because the new sign and the marking are changes that were not in the specification. The third room is closed to you. The yellow marking is treated as a changed condition, so you stop at the marking and do not step over it. You record the door position, the time and the marking from where you stand, route back the way you came, and ask the laboratory staff for a written revision. Until the revision arrives, you do not clean the corridor, including the parts you could reach from the middle. The point of the example is that a booking covers a plan, and a plan does not cover a changed room.

procedure: Stop when a new hazard sign appears that is not in the service specification, or when the room differs from the plan.
Move back to a safe position and do not approach the sign, the door or any container.
Record the sign's location, its position, what it shows in general terms, and the time, from a safe distance.
Check the laboratory hazard map with site management, if available, and note any difference from what you can see.
Route away, keep other people clear where you safely can, and do not wait in a hazard path.
Ask the laboratory staff to revise the cleaning boundary in writing, naming the open and closed areas and the decision maker.
Resume only when the site authority has given an updated scope, and clean only the areas it names as open.
Record the stop, the request and the revised scope on the job file, and leave the handover to housekeeping only.

workedExamples.situation: A corridor has new biohazard signage that is not in the service specification. The booking for the corridor is for this morning.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do first, what do you record, and when can the corridor be cleaned?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop at a distance and route away without approaching the sign. Record the sign's location, its position on the door, the time, and what you can see of it from where you stand. Do not try to identify the hazard. Ask the laboratory staff to revise the boundary in writing. The booking does not override the changed condition, so the corridor is not cleaned until the site authority gives an updated scope that names the open areas. If the revised scope excludes the corridor, the job is recorded as deferred, and the reason is the changed condition, not the cleaner's time or the booking.

workedExamples.situation: On the way to a laboratory bench you notice a chemical store with a new hazard sign on its door. The door is ajar and the room is not on the plan you were given.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and what documents do you ask for before any work near the store?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not look through the gap in the door. Record the sign and the door's position from a distance, and note that the room is not on the plan. Ask the laboratory staff for the hazardous chemicals register and the safety data sheets for the store, and ask whether the site keeps a register that is readily accessible to workers. The Safe Work Australia guidance says the register must be readily accessible to workers, must cover hazardous chemicals used, handled or stored at the workplace, and must have a current safety data sheet for each entry. Even when a register is available, do not enter the store or handle its contents. Wait for an updated scope that names the room.

workedExamples.situation: A sign on a fume hood reads that the hood is not to be cleaned, but the hood is not on the plan and the booking lists the whole bench.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you separate the parts of the bench you may clean from the part you may not?
workedExamples.reasoning: Treat the whole bench as changed until the site confirms otherwise. Record the sign, the hood, the bench and the time from a distance. Ask the laboratory staff to mark the bench in writing, showing the hood and any margin around it as excluded, and the parts that are open. A clear boundary on paper is the only basis for dividing the bench, not a guess about which parts look safe. Do not clean any area that the marking has not cleared.

equipmentAndPpe: Laboratory hazard map and the site's current service specification, if available.
Incident or deferral record form, with a space for sign location, time and people informed.
Written boundary revision request template, supplied by the site or the cleaning business.

Site-approved personal protective equipment for the approved housekeeping task only. Personal protective equipment is the last line of control and does not make entry to a marked area acceptable. The Safe Work Australia guidance describes personal protective equipment as one of the least effective control measures, to be used only after higher-level controls such as removing or substituting the hazard.
A means of contacting the laboratory supervisor or site management that does not require you to enter the area.

commonErrors.error: Reading a new sign as meaning the area is open, or as meaning it is safe to clean the parts you can reach.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat a new sign as a changed condition, stop, and ask for a written boundary before any part of the affected area is touched.

commonErrors.error: Approaching the sign to read it closely, or looking through a door panel or gap.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the location and the sign's general appearance from a safe distance, and do not look into the room.

commonErrors.error: Cleaning the corridor because the job is booked and the plan has not been updated.
commonErrors.prevention: A booking does not override a changed condition. Ask for the revised scope before any work.

commonErrors.error: Working out the hazard from the sign's colour or symbol and deciding that it is minor.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not interpret the hazard. Report it, and let the laboratory staff decide the risk and the boundary.

commonErrors.error: Recording only that a sign was seen, with no location, time or observer.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the location, the time, the observer, the people informed and the decision requested on every deferral record.

commonErrors.error: Taking photographs inside the area to show the sign.
commonErrors.prevention: Photograph only the outside of the door, and only if the site allows it. Do not enter to photograph.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Hazard signage marks a controlled condition, and this lesson does not authorise entry to the area the sign marks. Check the rules that apply in the state or territory where the site is located.

The Safe Work Australia guidance on hazardous chemicals says the hazardous chemicals register must be readily accessible to workers, that each entry needs a current safety data sheet, and that safety information for chemicals, hazardous or not, must be available to people at the workplace. Where a sign points to a chemical area, ask for this information before any work near it.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission states that claims about a business's services must be accurate and based on reasonable grounds, and that a business must be able to prove the claims it makes. This applies to advertising, quotes, staff statements and websites. A handover that describes an area as safe, sterile or cleared is a claim that needs evidence.

This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist. Work in hazardous areas that is licensed or restricted is outside the cleaner's authority unless the site gives a written scope for it and the cleaner is trained and equipped for it.

qualityStandard: New sign or changed condition identified as a stop, in the case study, before any part of the area is touched.
Location, time and observation recorded from a safe distance, with no approach to the sign or the door.
Written boundary revision requested, naming the open areas, the closed areas and the decision maker.
No cleaning resumed until a written, updated scope has been given, and only the areas it names are cleaned.
Handover describes housekeeping only, with no claim of sterility, decontamination or clearance.
documentationEvidence: Deferral record with sign location, description from a distance, time, observer and people informed.
Written request to revise the cleaning boundary, with the decision requested.
Revised scope from the site authority, with the open and closed areas named and the date and time of the decision.
Handover record stating housekeeping done, areas not touched and any exclusions.
summary: A new sign is a changed condition, and a changed condition stops the task until it is resolved.
Record from a safe distance, without approaching the sign or looking into the room.
Ask for a revised boundary in writing and clean only the areas it names as open.
Handover describes housekeeping only and never implies sterility or clearance.

knowledgeChecks.question: You find a new biohazard sign on a door that is not in the service specification. What is correct?
options: Read it as permission to continue with the rest of the corridor
Stop, record its location from a safe distance and ask for a revised boundary
Walk in to check what the sign applies to before deciding anything

knowledgeChecks.question: What should happen before the corridor is cleaned again?
options: Nothing, because the job was booked for this morning and the booking stands
The cleaner decides which parts of the corridor look safe to clean
The site authority gives an updated scope in writing that names the open areas
The cleaner waits for the sign to be removed by the site staff in their own time

knowledgeChecks.question: Can the handover say the corridor is sterile after the floor has been cleaned?
options: Yes, once the floor has been cleaned and the surfaces are dry to the touch
No, the handover covers housekeeping only, with no sterilisation or clearance claim
Yes, if the sign has been taken down from the door by the site staff this week

knowledgeChecks.question: A sign is posted beside a door you can see from the corridor. Where should you record the sign's location?
options: From inside the room, so the position is clear and the sign can be read easily
From a safe distance in the corridor, noting the door, the sign's position and the time
Photographed through the gap in the door, so the sign can be seen clearly from the corridor
